title: Predicting a probability
objectives: Fit a logistic regression and read its coefficients as odds
Turn log-odds into probabilities and back
Explain why a straight line cannot predict a probability

screens.prose: We have 400 business loans in the order they were made. Each defaulted (1) or did not (0). The line is the least-squares fit of default on **interest cover** over the first 300 loans: $\hat y = 0.472 - 0.0571 \times \text{cover}$.

state.caption: Orange: defaulted (1). Blue: repaid (0). Dots are nudged up or down a little so they do not overlap.

screens.question: What does the line predict for a loan with interest cover 10?

hints.text: Put cover = 10 into the equation.
$0.0571 \times 10 = 0.571$, and that is larger than the intercept.

feedback.correct: The line predicts −0.099 for a loan with cover 10.

byKey.sign: You dropped the minus sign. The intercept 0.472 is smaller than 0.571, so the result is negative.
byKey.clip: You stopped at 0 because a chance cannot be negative. The line does not know that: it gives −0.099.

explain.text: You found $0.472 - 0.571 = -0.099$, a negative chance of default. The line crosses 0 at cover 8.3 and keeps falling. A straight line has no reason to stay inside $[0, 1]$.

screens.prose: We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1. Slide $z$ along the S-curve $p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$. The caption also shows the **odds** $p/(1-p)$, as in the conditional course.
screens.question: Move $z$ from 0 to 1, then from 1 to 2. What happens to the odds each time?

options.text: They are multiplied by about 2.72 each time
They go up by the same amount each time
options.why: You compared the odds by subtracting: 1 to 2.72 is +1.72, but 2.72 to 7.39 is +4.67. The ratio is what stays fixed.

options.text: $p$ goes up by the same amount each time
options.why: $p$ went from 0.5 to 0.731, then to 0.881: steps of 0.231 and 0.150. The S-curve flattens as it nears 1.
From 1 to 2.72 is more than double. The factor is $e \approx 2.718$.

hints.text: Read the odds at $z = 0$, 1 and 2.
At $z = 0$ the odds are 1. Divide the next reading by it.
The odds read 1, 2.718 and 7.389. Each is the last one times 2.718.

feedback.correct: Each step of 1 in $z$ multiplies the odds by $e$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the odds at $z = 0$, 1 and 2, then divide each by the one before.

explain.text: You saw the odds go 1, 2.72, 7.39: each step of 1 in $z$ multiplied them by $e$. So the odds are $e^z$, and $z$ is the log of the odds.

screens.prose: So $z = \ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}$, the **log-odds**, and the S-curve $\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ is the **sigmoid**. It turns any log-odds back into a probability. The scale below spaces probabilities by their log-odds.
screens.question: A loan has a 0.2 chance of default. What are its log-odds?

hints.text: First turn the probability into odds.
The odds are $0.2/0.8 = 0.25$.
Take the natural log: $\ln 0.25 = -1.386$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the odds $p/(1-p)$ first, then take the natural log.

byKey.odds: 0.25 is the odds. The log-odds is its natural log.
byKey.lnp: You took the log of $p$. The log-odds is the log of $p/(1-p)$.
byKey.sign: A probability below 0.5 has odds below 1, so its log-odds are negative.

explain.text: You turned 0.2 into odds of 0.25 and took the log: −1.386. Below 0.5 the log-odds are negative; at 0.5 they are 0. The scale stretches near 0 and 1, where small changes in $p$ are large changes in log-odds.

screens.prose: **Logistic regression** makes the log-odds a straight line in the features. Fitted on the first 300 loans with leverage (debt over earnings), interest cover and loan size (standardised): $$\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = -1.960 + 0.601\,\text{lev} - 0.536\,\text{cover} + 0.023\,\text{size}$$

hints.text: Work out the log-odds $z$ first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $z$ from the equation, then $p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$.

byKey.z: −0.360 is the log-odds. Put it through the sigmoid to get a probability.

explain.text: You computed the log-odds, −0.360, and squeezed it through the sigmoid to get 0.411. Every logistic prediction is these two steps. The model is linear in log-odds, never in $p$.

screens.prose: Raise leverage by 1, holding the rest fixed. The log-odds rise by 0.601, so the odds are multiplied by $e^{0.601}$. That factor is the **odds ratio**.

A negative coefficient gives a factor below 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each cell is $e$ raised to that row's coefficient.

byKey.r0c2: $e^{0.601} = 1.824$: one more turn of leverage multiplies the odds of default by 1.824.
byKey.r1c2: $e^{-0.536} = 0.585$: one more turn of cover cuts the odds of default by 41.5%.

explain.text: Leverage multiplies the odds of default by 1.824 per turn; cover multiplies them by 0.585. Loan size gives 1.023, almost 1: the data were simulated with no size effect at all. A coefficient of 0 means an odds ratio of 1, no effect.

hints.text: Each loan moves 0.601 to the right on the S-curve.
A starts at log-odds $\ln(0.05/0.95) = -2.944$; B starts at 0.

feedback.correct: A rises by 0.038 and B by 0.146: same log-odds step, different probability steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move each loan 0.601 along the log-odds axis and read the new $p$.

byKey.adds: You read 0.601 as a change in probability. It is a change in log-odds: B would reach 1.101, which is impossible.

explain.text: Both loans moved 0.601 to the right on the S-curve. A sits on the flat tail and gains 0.038; B sits on the steep middle and gains 0.146. A coefficient is a change in log-odds; what it does to $p$ depends on where you start.

screens.prose: How does scikit-learn choose the coefficients? By **maximum likelihood**, as in the estimation course: the $\boldsymbol\beta$ that make the observed defaults most likely. Loan $i$ has model probability $p_i$ and outcome $y_i$, 1 or 0.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P(Y_i = y_i) = p_i^{\,y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}$: one loan is a Bernoulli trial
$L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \prod_i p_i^{\,y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}$: loans are independent, so chances multiply
$\ln L = \sum_i \left[y_i \ln p_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - p_i)\right]$: the log turns the product into a sum
Minimise $-\tfrac{1}{n}\ln L$, the **log loss**: the smallest loss is the largest likelihood

hints.text: Start with a single loan.
A product over loans needs independence; the log comes after the product.
One loan, then the product, then its log, then flip the sign to get a loss.

feedback.correct: One Bernoulli trial, a product, a log, a loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build from one loan to all of them before taking logs.

byKey.prod: The product comes after one loan's probability is written down.
byKey.log: Take the log of the whole product, so it comes after the product line.
byKey.loss: The loss is the negative log-likelihood, so it comes last.

explain.text: With $y_i = 1$ the first line gives $p_i$, and with $y_i = 0$ it gives $1 - p_i$. Logs turn the product of 300 small numbers into a sum we can minimise. scikit-learn also adds a ridge-style penalty, set by `C`, exactly as in level 2.

widget.solution:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def fit_logistic_proba(X_train, y_train, X_query):
    model = LogisticRegression(C=1.0)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    probs = model.predict_proba(X_query)[:, 1]
    return [round(float(v), 4) for v in probs]
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 400
lev = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 7.5, n), 2)
cover = np.round(np.clip(rng.gamma(3.0, 1.3, n), 0.2, 12), 2)
size = np.round(rng.normal(0, 1, n), 2)
z = -2.0 + 0.6 * lev - 0.55 * cover
default = (rng.uniform(0, 1, n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
X = np.column_stack([lev, cover, size])
X_train, y_train = X[:300], default[:300]
X_test, y_test = X[300:], default[300:]

tests.call: sum(v > 0.5 for v in fit_logistic_proba(X_train, y_train, X_test))

screens.prose: A credit desk prices a one-year loan from its probability of default (PD). A rough rule: the spread over the risk-free rate is PD times the share of the loan lost in default. The model gives a borrower log-odds of −3.15. The desk expects to lose 60% in default.
screens.question: What spread does the rule give, in basis points?

hints.text: Turn the log-odds into a probability first.
$0.0411 \times 0.6 = 0.0247$, which is 247 basis points.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put −3.15 through the sigmoid, then multiply by 0.6.

byKey.odds: You used $e^{-3.15} = 0.0429$, the odds. The rule needs the probability, $0.0429/1.0429 = 0.0411$.
byKey.no-lgd: That is the PD alone in basis points. The desk loses only 60% of the loan in default.

explain.text: You turned −3.15 into a PD of 0.0411 and scaled by the 60% loss: 247 bp. For a rare event the odds and the probability are close, 0.0429 against 0.0411. That gap is 10 bp of spread, which is real money on a large loan.

ideas: A straight line for a 0/1 target runs outside $[0, 1]$; logistic regression makes the log-odds linear instead.
A coefficient is a change in log-odds: one unit multiplies the odds by $e^{\beta}$, and the change in $p$ depends on where you start.
The fit maximises the likelihood, which is minimising log loss; `predict` is `predict_proba` cut at 0.5, a choice.

formula.name: Logistic regression
formula.note: Linear in log-odds, S-shaped in probability.

summary.trap: Reading a coefficient as a change in probability: it changes the log-odds, so its effect on $p$ is largest near 0.5.

quiz.prose: A desk's model gives a 0.52 chance that a share rises tomorrow. Over the last year, 53% of the share's days were up days.
quiz.question: What does the 0.52 tell you on its own?

options.text: Little: it is below the 53% of days that rise anyway, and we do not know if it is calibrated

options.why: You compared 0.52 with a coin. Up days are already 53% of days, so 0.52 is a slightly bearish call.

options.text: The odds of an up day are 0.52
options.why: Odds are $p/(1-p) = 0.52/0.48 = 1.083$. And odds would not settle the trading question either.
A probability for one day is not an accuracy over many days. Accuracy needs a test set.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 0.52 with how often the share rises anyway.

explain.text: Up days are 53% of days, so 'up with chance 0.52' is no better than the base rate. Lesson 14 tests such claims properly. Lesson 13 asks whether a model's 0.52 really means 52%.

quiz.prose: In a small training set every defaulted loan has leverage above 5 and every repaid loan has leverage below 5. You fit logistic regression with no penalty at all.
quiz.question: What happens to the leverage coefficient?

options.text: It grows without limit: a steeper S-curve always fits these loans better
It settles where the boundary sits at leverage 5
options.why: The boundary does settle near 5, but the slope keeps growing. A steeper S-curve gives each loan a probability nearer its outcome, so the likelihood keeps rising.

options.text: It goes to 0, because there is no uncertainty left
options.why: Perfect separation pushes the fit the other way: the S-curve wants to become a step, which needs an infinite slope.

options.text: Nothing unusual: scikit-learn returns a finite number
options.why: With its default penalty, `C=1.0`, it does. That penalty hides the problem; with no penalty the optimiser runs off.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what makes the likelihood larger when the classes do not overlap.

explain.text: When the classes separate perfectly, a steeper curve always raises the likelihood, so the unpenalised maximum is at infinity. scikit-learn's default `C=1.0` penalty stops at a finite slope and hides the problem.

quiz.prose: In our model, interest cover has coefficient −0.536.
quiz.question: By what factor do the odds of default change when cover rises by 2?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two units add $2 \times (-0.536)$ to the log-odds.

byKey.one: 0.585 is the factor for one unit of cover. Two units apply it twice: $0.585^2 = 0.342$.
byKey.double: You doubled the odds ratio. Two units multiply by it twice, so square it.
byKey.lin: −1.072 is the change in log-odds. The odds change by $e^{-1.072}$.

explain.text: Two units of cover add $2 \times (-0.536) = -1.072$ to the log-odds. So the odds are multiplied by $e^{-1.072} = 0.342$, which is $0.585^2$.

quiz.prose: A model for a 3% default rate gives no loan a probability above 0.40. You call `model.predict` on 1,000 new loans.
quiz.question: How many loans does `predict` flag as defaults?

byKey.rate: You expected the base rate, 30 loans. `predict` cuts at 0.5, and no loan gets there.

explain.text: With rare defaults, probabilities rarely reach 0.5, so `predict` says no to everyone. The ranking inside `predict_proba` may still be useful. Lesson 11 picks a threshold that fits the costs.
